THIS NOTEBOOK DOES NOT REPORT HUMAN RESEARCH RESULTS. All figures are deterministic synthetic models; no claim of qigong-specific energy, quantum entanglement, or clinical efficacy is established. Five-flagship genealogy and independent endpoints F041 | Human Infrared Emission Spectra and Skin Temperature at the Limit Native endpoint: infrared spectral radiance residual [W/(m2 sr um)]; strong baseline: rest-matched condition; primary conventional rival: ambient reflection and detector gain. Core physical account: band-resolved Planck radiance with emissivity and reflected apparent temperature. Independent witness: a temperature-stabilized blackbody in the same optical path. The required handoff is to transfer the cavity calibration, spectral response function and radiance covariance matrix. F042 | Pre-Post Qigong Thermal Mapping and Environmental Correction at the Limit Native endpoint: ambient-corrected thermal-map change [K]; strong baseline: movement- and breathing-matched condition; primary conventional rival: airflow, acclimatization and postural shifts. Core physical account: radiative transfer plus convection, evaporation and thermal relaxation. Independent witness: a movement-matched control under the same airflow and camera geometry. The required handoff is to publish raw radiometric frames, registration landmarks and the difference-in-differences estimator. F043 | Human Skin Emissivity and Surface Material Properties at the Limit Native endpoint: skin emissivity residual [dimensionless]; strong baseline: temperature- and moisture-matched reference; primary conventional rival: surface films, humidity and viewing angle. Core physical account: energy conservation at an absorbing, emitting and reflecting boundary. Independent witness: a traceable high-emissivity reference of documented surface treatment. The required handoff is to report bandpass, angular response, film history and covariance between inferred temperature and emissivity. F044 | Palmar Thermal Emission and Local Blood Flow Coupling at the Limit Native endpoint: temperature-perfusion temporal lag [s]; strong baseline: rest and sham-synchronized sensor record; primary conventional rival: probe motion, posture and shared respiratory drive. Core physical account: vascular heat transport convolved with tissue thermal diffusion. Independent witness: a shared-clock perfusion trace plus a motion and respiration record. The required handoff is to release synchronization pulses, surrogate distributions and bilateral negative controls. F045 | Human Thermography and Blinded Image Classification at the Limit Native endpoint: external-site blinded thermography AUC [0-1]; strong baseline: metadata-only and site-heldout classifiers; primary conventional rival: background leakage, identity overlap and domain shift. Core physical account: statistical generalization under a documented distribution shift. Independent witness: an operator- and person-heldout external test with masked class labels. The required handoff is to release split keys, model weights, inference preprocessing, abstention rule and confusion matrices.

summary: This record contains the raw data generated in the computational experiments of the article "EpiBuilder 2.0: A Dockerized and User-Friendly Web Platform for in silico Analysis of Linear B-cell Epitopes" . Source code: https://github.com/labioinfoufsc/EpiBuilder . The data were used to (i) benchmark the processing time of the EpiBuilder 2.0 workflow on CPU and GPU on two different machines, (ii) compare the epitope predictor integrated into EpiBuilder 2.0 (BepiPred v3.0) with an alternative deep-learning predictor (EpiDope v0.3), in processing time and in per-residue concordance, and (iii) carry out the biological evaluation of the predicted linear B-cell epitopes (N-glycosylation filtering, subcellular localization, BLASTp matches against the IEDB and against other proteomes of the same genus). All runs were performed in triplicate . The archive contains only the generated outputs and the shell scripts used to produce them; the input proteomes are public UniProt reference proteomes and are not redistributed. Hardware configurations Machine A (Intel Core i9-14900K @ 6.0 GHz, 80 GB DDR5 6000 MHz): configuration A – CPU only ( machine_A/cpu/ ); A1 – NVIDIA RTX 3080, 10 GB ( machine_A/RTX_3080/ ); A2 – NVIDIA RTX A4500, 20 GB ( machine_A/RTX_A4500/ ). Machine B (Intel Xeon E7-4830 v2 @ 2.20 GHz, 295 GB DDR3 1600 MHz): configuration B – CPU only ( machine_B/cpu/ ). Input proteomes (UniProt, downloaded on 6 November 2026) Influenza B virus B/Lee/1940 – UP000008158 (11 proteins) Zaire ebolavirus – UP000007209 (9 proteins) Borrelia burgdorferi B31 – UP000001807 (1,273 valid proteins) Staphylococcus aureus – UP000008816 (2,888 valid proteins) Candida albicans – UP000000559 (5,977 valid proteins) Software and parameters BepiPred v3.0 (Docker image bioinfoufsc/bepipred3 ), CPU and GPU. EpiDope v0.3 ( flomock/epidope:v0.3 ), CPU only. EpiBuilder 2.0 core workflow in Nextflow ( bioinfoufsc/epibuilder-core ): epitope extraction, physicochemical properties, N-glycosylation, PSORTb v3.0 / WoLF PSORT v0.1, BLASTp v2.17 against the IEDB (~155,279 B-cell epitopes) and reference proteomes of each genus. Parameters: epitope length 10–30 aa; BepiPred v3.0 threshold 0.1512; BLAST minimum identity 90% and minimum query coverage 90%; localization none (viruses), gram_neg ( B. burgdorferi ), gram_pos ( S. aureus ), fungi ( C. albicans ). Contents of EpiBuilder2_experiments.tar.gz scripts/ – experiment_bepipred.sh (BepiPred v3.0, CPU or GPU), experiment_epidope.sh (EpiDope v0.3), experiment.sh (one EpiBuilder 2.0 run) and experiment_triplicate.sh (loop over organisms and replicates). machine_A/ and machine_B/ – one folder per configuration and tool ( bepipred , epidope , epibuilder ), with one subfolder per organism ( INFLUENZA , EBOLA , BORRELIA , STAPHYLOCOCCUS , CANDIDA ) and replicate1 – replicate3 . bepipred/ – FASTA validation output, per-residue scores ( raw_output.csv ), execution logs and wall-clock times ( execution_times.tsv ). epidope/ – per-residue scores ( epidope_scores.csv ), predicted epitopes, per-protein tables and plots, and execution times. epibuilder/ – epitope-level results ( epitope-detail.tsv , epitopes.fasta ), per-protein summary, per-residue scores, subcellular localization, BLASTp hits against the IEDB and each reference proteome, consolidated spreadsheet ( epibuilder.xlsx ) and Nextflow trace, report, timeline and DAG ( reports/ ). Use in the publication CPU vs. GPU processing time of the workflow (configurations A, A1, A2 and B) and comparison between machines: bepipred/*/execution_times.tsv and epibuilder/*/replicateN/reports/trace.txt . BepiPred v3.0 vs. EpiDope v0.3 processing time on CPU: execution_times.tsv of both tools. Per-residue concordance between BepiPred v3.0 and EpiDope v0.3 (Cohen's kappa, Jaccard index, Spearman's rho): raw_output.csv and epidope_scores.csv . Biological evaluation, IEDB matches and cross-species

summary: This record contains the raw data generated in the computational experiments of the article "EpiBuilder 2.0: A Dockerized and User-Friendly Web Platform for in silico Analysis of Linear B-cell Epitopes" . Source code: https://github.com/labioinfoufsc/EpiBuilder . The data were used to (i) benchmark the processing time of the EpiBuilder 2.0 workflow on CPU and GPU on two different machines, (ii) compare the epitope predictor integrated into EpiBuilder 2.0 (BepiPred v3.0) with an alternative deep-learning predictor (EpiDope v0.3), in processing time and in per-residue concordance, and (iii) carry out the biological evaluation of the predicted linear B-cell epitopes (N-glycosylation filtering, subcellular localization, BLASTp matches against the IEDB and against other proteomes of the same genus). All runs were performed in triplicate . The archive contains only the generated outputs and the shell scripts used to produce them; the input proteomes are public UniProt reference proteomes and are not redistributed. Hardware configurations Machine A (Intel Core i9-14900K @ 6.0 GHz, 80 GB DDR5 6000 MHz): configuration A – CPU only ( machine_A/cpu/ ); A1 – NVIDIA RTX 3080, 10 GB ( machine_A/RTX_3080/ ); A2 – NVIDIA RTX A4500, 20 GB ( machine_A/RTX_A4500/ ). Machine B (Intel Xeon E7-4830 v2 @ 2.20 GHz, 295 GB DDR3 1600 MHz): configuration B – CPU only ( machine_B/cpu/ ). Input proteomes (UniProt, downloaded on 6 November 2026) Influenza B virus B/Lee/1940 – UP000008158 (11 proteins) Zaire ebolavirus – UP000007209 (9 proteins) Borrelia burgdorferi B31 – UP000001807 (1,273 valid proteins) Staphylococcus aureus – UP000008816 (2,888 valid proteins) Candida albicans – UP000000559 (5,977 valid proteins) Software and parameters BepiPred v3.0 (Docker image bioinfoufsc/bepipred3 ), CPU and GPU. EpiDope v0.3 ( flomock/epidope:v0.3 ), CPU only. EpiBuilder 2.0 core workflow in Nextflow ( bioinfoufsc/epibuilder-core ): epitope extraction, physicochemical properties, N-glycosylation, PSORTb v3.0 / WoLF PSORT v0.1, BLASTp v2.17 against the IEDB (~155,279 B-cell epitopes) and reference proteomes of each genus. Parameters: epitope length 10–30 aa; BepiPred v3.0 threshold 0.1512; BLAST minimum identity 90% and minimum query coverage 90%; localization none (viruses), gram_neg ( B. burgdorferi ), gram_pos ( S. aureus ), fungi ( C. albicans ). Contents of EpiBuilder2_experiments.tar.gz scripts/ – experiment_bepipred.sh (BepiPred v3.0, CPU or GPU), experiment_epidope.sh (EpiDope v0.3), experiment.sh (one EpiBuilder 2.0 run) and experiment_triplicate.sh (loop over organisms and replicates). machine_A/ and machine_B/ – one folder per configuration and tool ( bepipred , epidope , epibuilder ), with one subfolder per organism ( INFLUENZA , EBOLA , BORRELIA , STAPHYLOCOCCUS , CANDIDA ) and replicate1 – replicate3 . bepipred/ – FASTA validation output, per-residue scores ( raw_output.csv ), execution logs and wall-clock times ( execution_times.tsv ). epidope/ – per-residue scores ( epidope_scores.csv ), predicted epitopes, per-protein tables and plots, and execution times. epibuilder/ – epitope-level results ( epitope-detail.tsv , epitopes.fasta ), per-protein summary, per-residue scores, subcellular localization, BLASTp hits against the IEDB and each reference proteome, consolidated spreadsheet ( epibuilder.xlsx ) and Nextflow trace, report, timeline and DAG ( reports/ ). Use in the publication CPU vs. GPU processing time of the workflow (configurations A, A1, A2 and B) and comparison between machines: bepipred/*/execution_times.tsv and epibuilder/*/replicateN/reports/trace.txt . BepiPred v3.0 vs. EpiDope v0.3 processing time on CPU: execution_times.tsv of both tools. Per-residue concordance between BepiPred v3.0 and EpiDope v0.3 (Cohen's kappa, Jaccard index, Spearman's rho): raw_output.csv and epidope_scores.csv . summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph on $n$ vertices with minimum degree $m\ge3$ and maximum degree $M$, and put $Q=M/(m-1)$. A non-backtracking random walk of length $k$ on $G$, started along any directed edge, is vertex-simple with probability at most $256\,Q(1+Q)\,n/k^2$. Hence the conjecture of Alon and Peres, that a non-backtracking walk of length $C(\varepsilon)\sqrt n$ self-intersects with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$, holds with $C(\varepsilon)$ depending only on $\varepsilon$ and a bound for $M/m$; for regular graphs of degree at least three one may take $C(\varepsilon)=31\varepsilon^{-1/2}$ for every degree. The expected self-intersection time is at most $32\sqrt{Q(1+Q)n}+2$, which removes the logarithmic factor from the bound of Bencs et al.\ for graphs of minimum degree at least three and bounded maximum degree. The proof adapts Dozier's argument for regular graphs: departures are weighted by the inverse branching at their vertex, and the deviating local derangement is resampled.
title: A birthday bound for non-backtracking walks on graphs of bounded degree ratio

summary: Identifying refugia, areas likely to be buffered from climate change, is an important wildlife conservation strategy. For forest-associated wildlife, better representation of climate conditions should improve refugia identification. We quantified refugia potential for boreal songbirds in Alberta, Canada, by comparing distribution models based on macroclimate (unadjusted) and locally downscaled climate predictions (microclimate). We surveyed songbirds with autonomous recording units (n = 2147 locations) from spring to mid-summer between 2014 and 2018 and recorded air temperature with iButton Thermochron dataloggers (n = 283) in river valleys and hills systems. Using microclimate offsets, we downscaled macroclimate based on topography and vegetation cover. We fit boosted regression tree (BRT) models for 48 forest songbird species using four model combinations: climate-only models with (i) downscaled vs. (ii) unadjusted climate, and climate + vegetation (full model) with downscaled (iii) vs. (iv) unadjusted climate. F or each species, we compared the four model combinations in terms of predictive performance, variable importance, and projected refugia potential, and summarized the results by nesting habitat group (coniferous, deciduous, and wetland). . For most species, vegetation variables (relative biomass of key tree species) had lower importance in bird models based on downscaled climate, suggesting a degree of substitutability. However, model explanatory power did not improve with downscaled climate variables for most species. Coniferous-associated species were the exception, suggesting greater sensitivity to local climate conditions. We then predicted refugia potential as the area of overlap between current and projected future distribution under a moderate climate scenario. Climate-only models predicted less habitat loss for coniferous species using downscaled climate (21% habitat loss vs. 58% loss with unadjusted variables), whereas full models with vegetation showed the reverse, with greater habitat loss under downscaled climate (39% downscaled vs. 23% with unadjusted climate variables). For deciduous-associated species, which were mostly projected to increase under climate change, habitat loss was smaller using downscaled climate regardless of model type. Overall, our results suggest that microclimate downscaling improves the identification of refugia for coniferous-associated species in this region.   Managers should consider targeting areas with high refugia potential to improve conservation outcomes.
title: Data from: Downscaling climate models with vegetation and topography identifies refugia for some, but not all, boreal songbirds

summary: Agentic ecosystems are emerging as a new platform layer in which agents maintain persistent memory, retrieve from shared knowledge bases, execute through tool interfaces, and coordinate through shared states. These capabilities create a security problem that per-turn defenses miss: compromise can accumulate across sessions, agents, and system layers before visible failure. We define this threat as Agentic Sleeper, a system-level adversary that first behaves legitimately, gains routing trust, and later activates across memory, agent logic, and infrastructure. We formulate defense as inference under partial observability and propose Swarm Shepherd, a system-level defense framework centered on an inference filter for early warning, paired with a backward trace-back module for entry attribution. Our analysis yields a two-scale deployment rule that balances longer event histories against broader agent coverage. Across LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen, Agentic Sleeper drift begins 2.7--8.9$\times$ faster than natural baselines, propagates across agents on most topologies, and evades per-turn and stateful defenses above 80\%. Swarm Shepherd warns at least three sessions before visible degradation (2.6 sessions when failure is scored by the benchmark's own task grader), while trace-back reaches 0.69 top-1 accuracy and 0.72 macro-F1 over 24 variants. The two-scale deployment rule is empirically confirmed, and in live end-to-end runs on LangGraph and AutoGen the posterior-guided defense stack drives cross-agent propagation below the self-sustaining regime, which removing only the visibly compromised agent does not achieve.
title: Swarm Shepherd: Securing Multi-Agent Ecosystems Against Persistent Latent Compromise

summary: On-ramp merging is a typical safety and throughput problem on highways. Without proper coordination, human drivers and self-interested autonomous vehicles may make risky manoeuvres and cause accidents or congestion. With recent advances in connected autonomous vehicles (CAVs) and multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), vehicles can be trained to coordinate for safe and efficient merging. However, in dense traffic, forming an effective observation of the traffic state is challenging. For example, observing only the neighbouring vehicles may lead to locally optimal decisions, while observing the entire traffic can introduce much irrelevant information. In this paper, we propose a transformer-based MARL vehicle control model to address these problems. A roadside infrastructure controller receives the states of all CAVs via vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) communication and sends control commands back to them. An attention-based observation encoder is designed where each vehicle can filter the relevant vehicle information from the global traffic state. The proposed model is evaluated in SUMO against three baselines: a model that observes only the neighbouring vehicles, a model that encodes the global traffic information, and the rule-based SUMO model. The results show that our model achieves the highest traffic flow, safety and smoothness. Furthermore, in a four-hour simulation with dynamic traffic demand, our model successfully avoids traffic jams, while other baseline models fail at high traffic flow. We also show that our model remains effective when human-driven vehicles are present. We further show that our model, trained in ideal communication conditions, can still remain collision-free and maintain throughput under realistic V2I communication errors. Finally, we visualise the relevance weights that an ego vehicle assigns to other vehicles in multiple traffic situations.
title: Infrastructure-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Attention for Highway Ramp Merging

summary: As agentic systems are increasingly deployed to support complex Web tasks, multi-agent architectures offer greater parallelism, specialization, and task coverage. However, increasing the number of agents does not necessarily improve system performance, as communication, synchronization, redundant work, and coordination overhead may offset the benefits of additional agents. This presents a fundamental scaling challenge for agentic Web systems: how can agent populations be organized to balance task performance and coordination costs? To address this challenge, we systematically investigate the relationship between agent population size, per-agent token consumption, and coordination overhead in collaborative agentic systems. Experiments on complex Web-oriented software development tasks reveal a non-linear scaling pattern: per-agent token consumption initially decreases as the agent population grows, but eventually exhibits diminishing returns. Motivated by these findings, we introduce the Surgical Team Model (STM), a structured coordination framework that organizes agents through role specialization, constrained inter-agent communication, and coordinator-mediated task aggregation. Experiments on full-stack Web application development tasks show that STM achieves competitive task completion quality and comparable token consumption relative to representative baselines, while incurring higher execution latency.
title: When the Mythical Man-Month Meets Agentic Web Systems: Structured Coordination for Scalable Development

summary: Reliable monitoring of astronauts is essential for safety, situational awareness, and autonomous assistance in space missions. While modern computer vision enables accurate human detection and pose estimation on Earth, its robustness in space environments remains largely unquantified due to limited data availability. We present AstroPIE-53, a pilot dataset of 53 annotated astronaut videos collected from publicly available mission footage. To respect copyright restrictions, we release video identifiers, reconstruction scripts, and dense annotations rather than raw videos. The dataset includes bounding boxes, challenge classes, and human-annotated pose failure tags. We benchmark state-of-the-art person detection and pose estimation models under realistic zero-shot deployment conditions and perform the first systematic failure analysis for astronaut monitoring. Our results reveal substantial performance degradation caused by occlusions, unusual body orientations, low contrast, and microgravity motion patterns.
title: AstroPIE-53: Towards Understanding Failure Modes of Human Pose Estimation in Space

summary: Subgroup heterogeneity in carryover effects is not routinely evaluated in 2x2 crossover studies, and its inferential consequences remain insufficiently characterized. When the scientific question concerns subgroup-specific carryover, omission of the corresponding interaction causes the fitted model to target a collapsed population-average contrast rather than the subgroup difference of interest. We used simulation to evaluate the finite-sample bias, confidence-interval coverage, Type I error, and power of carryover-by-subgroup interaction inference under an independence-based analysis and REML-based MMRM analyses with CS and UN covariance specifications. Reduced mean models were included as population-average benchmarks. We also applied the models to observational Alzheimer disease treatment-transition sequences from NACC, where carryover was defined operationally as a model-based association with the preceding regimen rather than an identified pharmacologic persistence effect. Full models directly estimated subgroup-specific carryover heterogeneity, whereas reduced models estimated a collapsed carryover contrast that did not characterize this heterogeneity. Under the full mean model, point-estimate bias was small, whereas covariance misspecification affected empirical confidence-interval coverage and Type I error. Reliable inference on subgroup-specific carryover effects requires a mean model that explicitly represents the heterogeneity of interest and a covariance structure appropriate for the repeated-measures data. Failure to address either component can obscure subgroup differences or compromise statistical inference. These results provide practical guidance for evaluating heterogeneous carryover effects in crossover and treatment-transition studies.
title: Assessing Subgroup Heterogeneity in Carryover Effects: A Simulation Study and an Observational Alzheimer Disease Treatment-Transition Application

summary: Subgroup heterogeneity in carryover effects is not routinely evaluated in 2x2 crossover studies, and its inferential consequences remain insufficiently characterized. When the scientific question concerns subgroup-specific carryover, omission of the corresponding interaction causes the fitted model to target a collapsed population-average contrast rather than the subgroup difference of interest. We used simulation to evaluate the finite-sample bias, confidence-interval coverage, Type I error, and power of carryover-by-subgroup interaction inference under an independence-based analysis and REML-based MMRM analyses with CS and UN covariance specifications. Reduced mean models were included as population-average benchmarks. We also applied the models to observational Alzheimer disease treatment-transition sequences from NACC, where carryover was defined operationally as a model-based association with the preceding regimen rather than an identified pharmacologic persistence effect. Full models directly estimated subgroup-specific carryover heterogeneity, whereas reduced models estimated a collapsed carryover contrast that did not characterize this heterogeneity. Under the full mean model, point-estimate bias was small, whereas covariance misspecification affected empirical confidence-interval coverage and Type I error. Reliable inference on subgroup-specific carryover effects requires a mean model that explicitly represents the heterogeneity of interest and a covariance structure appropriate for the repeated-measures data. Failure to address either component can obscure subgroup differences or compromise statistical inference. These results provide practical guidance for evaluating heterogeneous carryover effects in crossover and treatment-transition studies.
title: Assessing Subgroup Heterogeneity in Carryover Effects: A Simulation Study and an Observational Alzheimer Disease Treatment-Transition Application

summary: Knowledge-guided generative systems use explicit domain constraints to improve decision consistency and alignment with human-created solutions. However, locally valid decisions do not necessarily preserve contextual relationships in human decision-making. This paper examines when structural constraints improve or degrade agreement with human reference solutions. We introduce HARMONIX, an experimental framework using automated musical harmonization as a controlled testbed for knowledge-guided decision-making. Four configurations share the same Viterbi-based optimization mechanism: a baseline, repetition constraints, functional constraints, and their combination. Experiments cover 19,745 records and 143,634 motif pairs across training and validation partitions. Combined constraints improve reference root-interval agreement by approximately five percentage points in stable structural contexts but reduce it by nearly nine percentage points in contexts involving transposition tracking. These opposing effects are consistent across both partitions, while overall exact chord agreement changes only marginally. Contexts are identified retrospectively using reference annotations; no adaptive constraint-selection mechanism is evaluated. The findings demonstrate that interpretable constraints can introduce systematic context-specific failures concealed by aggregate accuracy metrics. They highlight the need to evaluate relationships between decisions and the contextual applicability of constraints in knowledge-guided generative systems.
title: When Valid Decisions Are Not Enough: Evaluating Structural Constraints in Knowledge-Guided Generative Systems

summary: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) improves language model reasoning by distilling from a frozen teacher initialized identically to the student and conditioned on privileged information. However, we identify an underexplored termination mismatch in OPSD: the student fails to reliably learn when to continue and when to stop. This mismatch manifests in two opposing failure modes-premature termination, where reasoning stops before sufficient progress is made, and repetition-driven over-generation, where the model continues generating after reasoning has stalled. Our analysis shows that the teacher-student discrepancy on EOS grows during OPSD training, while length-capped trajectories are frequently dominated by unproductive repetition. To address this issue, we propose TA-OPSD (Termination-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation), which augments the original OPSD objective with two targeted objectives. Stop/Continue Distillation addresses premature termination by explicitly aligning the teacher and student on whether reasoning should continue, while Repetition-Aware Unlikelihood Training addresses repetition-driven over-generation by discouraging repetitive continuations in the student's failed trajectories. The resulting objective improves termination behavior from complementary directions: continuing when further reasoning is needed and stopping when reasoning becomes unproductive. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks with Qwen3 (1.7B/4B/8B) show that TA-OPSD consistently outperforms OPSD and other baselines across all three model scales. Beyond the performance gains, ablation and behavioral analyses show that the two proposed objectives effectively mitigate their corresponding termination failures, reducing both premature termination and repetition-driven over-generation.
title: Learning When to Continue and When to Stop: Termination-Aware OPSD

summary: Many reinforcement learning methods tie data collection to the task policy, while coordinating independently optimized behavior and target policies remains challenging. Policies learned by these methods can perform unreliably in long-horizon tasks under uncertainty, such as inventory control, where failures can incur extreme costs. We introduce Heuristic Behavior Policy Optimization (HBPO), an off-policy framework that routes heuristic guidance through persistent behavior learning, coupled with target-policy, updating separately with residual-based advantage estimation and emphatic weighting. Under matched environment interaction budgets on DSIS and its risk-augmented variant DSIS-RB, HBPO recovers many high-cost initial policies and improves most non-collapse comparison groups. Cold starts achieve competitive costs without final cost collapse across all tested seeds. We identify a transmission chain in the delayed heuristic-behavior-target coupling as a key driver of recovery and improvement. Generation-level diagnostics trace heuristic uptake and subsequent selective target responses, while component ablations support the contribution of this transmission mechanism to policy recovery and improvement.
title: Delayed Heuristic-Behavior-Target Coupling for Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning in Inventory Control

summary: This note develops a provisional admissibility framework for Aharonov-Bohm type arbitrage. Starting from a categorical filtration $F:\mathcal T_{\mathrm{mic}}^{\mathrm{op}}\to \mathsf{Prob}$ and its distortion on microscopic histories, we ask when a favorable closed microscopic loop can be realized as an executable relative ordinal arbitrage over an open macro-time interval. The history endofunctor $\mathsf{Hist}$ retains the staged decomposition of economic activities, while the twisted-arrow category $\operatorname{Tw}(\mathsf{Hist}(\mathcal T_{\mathrm{mic}}))$ represents a microscopic loop as an arrow between distinct histories. An observable clock $Π: \mathsf{Econ} \to \mathcal T_{\mathrm{mac}}$ and a microscopic realization functor $J: \mathsf{Hist}(\mathcal T_{\mathrm{mac}}) \to \operatorname{Tw}(\mathsf{Hist}(\mathcal T_{\mathrm{mic}}))$ connect economic histories with their microscopic geometry. Executability is treated separately through configuration histories, capacity constraints, observations, and policies. This yields pathwise and almost-sure notions of execution. A finite foreign-exchange model illustrates stochastic execution, capacity failure, terminal settlement, and comparison with a benchmark strategy. A parameterized finite filtration is constructed whose nontrivial statewise distortion agrees exactly with the relative FX settlement multiplier. Hence the resulting filtration--policy model satisfies the bridge $V_*(π^q)=dF(γ)V_*(π^p),$ and, under order compatibility, realizes relative ordinal arbitrage. The remaining problem is to identify the filtration parameters from independent market primitives and to study stability under refinement.
title: Toward an Admissibility Theory of Aharonov--Bohm Arbitrage

summary: Denoising autoencoders have shown strong empirical performance in recovering clean data from their noisy observations, yet their underlying statistical behavior remains underexplored. In this paper, we study denoising autoencoders under the manifold hypothesis, assuming that clean data are supported on low-dimensional smooth manifolds embedded in a high-dimensional ambient space, while noisy observations are generated by isotropic Gaussian noise. We establish generalization guarantees in three geometric scenarios: a single manifold, a pairwise separated finite union of manifolds, and a finite union of intersecting manifolds. Using local chart representations, partitions of unity, and neural network approximation, we derive upper bounds for the expected squared reconstruction error for denoising autoencoder. In the single-manifold and separated-union scenarios, the error consists of a sample-dependent statistical term of order $n^{-2/(d+2)}\log^4 n$, a residual term of order $dσ^2/D$ caused by tangential noise, and an exponentially small tail term associated with failure of the manifold projection. Here $D$ is the data ambient dimension, $d$ is the intrinsic dimension of the clean-data manifold, and $σ^2$ is the expected squared noise magnitude. In the scenario of intersecting manifolds, we further identify an additional ambiguity term determined by the probability mass near the intersection neighborhood. Numerical experiments on synthetic manifolds and real image datasets support the predicted sample-size scaling law and illustrate the additional reconstruction ambiguity near manifold intersections.
title: A Geometric Understanding of Denoising Autoencoder with Applications to Image Denoising

summary: Effective planning requires representations that preserve task-relevant geometry and object identity while ignoring visual variation that does not alter the task. Existing evaluations of visual generalization often change several factors simultaneously, making the source of a failure difficult to identify. We introduce a controlled evaluation of object-goal navigation (ObjectNav), the task of reaching an instance of a named object category, in procedurally generated ProcTHOR houses. Training and evaluation houses share floor plans, object locations, goals, and start states, while visual factors are changed individually or in combination. Across model-free reinforcement learning (RL), model-based RL, and agents using frozen pretrained visual representations, our results show that appearance changes impair navigation, but their effects differ sharply by factor. Surface material changes account for most of the average change in success, whereas clutter and lighting have little effect. The magnitude of a global image statistics shift does not reliably predict performance: changing only the goal object's appearance can substantially impair an end-to-end agent despite a small image-level change. We found that a model based agent that plans over frozen features from the pretrained DINOv2 image encoder achieves the highest success (0.83) under the full shift, but remains sensitive to surface appearance. Our experiments reveal an important requirement for planning representations: they must separate invariant spatial task structure from appearance.
title: Toward Planning Representations That Separate Task Structure from Visual Content

summary: Large language models (LLMs) have proven promising for synthesising loop invariants, a long-standing obstacle to automated program verification. Yet, frontier LLMs are typically accessible only through third-party APIs, hampering reproducibility and local deployment. Small language models (SLMs) sidestep these obstacles but require task-specific fine-tuning, for which high-quality training data is needed. We present a failure-driven data curation method for fine-tuning language models to synthesise loop invariants. Inspired by mutation testing, our approach applies semantic mutation operators to ground-truth invariants, producing semantic mutants that induce verification failure. Each mutant is paired with verifier feedback and its ground-truth counterpart, yielding training examples for feedback-guided invariant refinement. Whereas the vast space of mutants is a long-standing burden in mutation testing, it becomes an asset when generating training data, multiplying the examples obtainable from a fixed set of verified programs. We implement our approach for Dafny, augmenting an existing synthetic dataset of verified programs, and introduce a framework that iteratively refines candidate invariants using verifier feedback. On 472 DafnyBench programs, our best-performing fine-tuned Gemma-4-E4B configuration verifies 50.8% of programs zero-shot, compared to 8.1% for the base model, a 6.3$\times$ improvement. Higher-order mutants prove more effective as training data than first-order mutants, and adding mutation-based examples to direct synthesis examples, in which invariants are removed rather than mutated, improves performance under iterative refinement. Our approach also transfers to Qwen3.5-4B, whose zero-shot verification rate rises from 9.3% to 53.6%.
title: Learning from Mutants: Teaching Small Language Models to Synthesise Loop Invariants

summary: Which depths in a new camera view are determined by finitely many source-depth measurements? Pointwise uncertainty bounds do not answer this question: unobserved geometry between samples can change which surface is encountered first. We study a bounded Lipschitz class of continuous source inverse-depth fields with interval observations and known camera pose. Building on classical Lipschitz envelopes, we characterize the exact set of attainable first-hit depths and construct a globally admissible scene for every value in that set. The set can be disconnected. We also give a necessary and sufficient test for several proposed depths to be first hits of one shared scene. An epipolar reduction uses scalar cone inequalities without enumerating surfaces. In a rectified model with source spacing $h$, interval half-width $\varepsilon$, baseline $b$, and slope bound $L$, we prove a sharp worst-case inverse-depth diameter of $\max\{Lh+2\varepsilon,2\varepsilon/(1-bL)\}$ when $bL<1$, subject to sufficient depth and domain range for attainment. Exact samples still give the sharp bound $Lh$ at $bL=1$, while above this threshold ambiguity need not vanish as sampling becomes arbitrarily dense. Any positive measurement uncertainty can destroy uniform stability at the critical threshold. We provide constructive examples, an exact rational validation oracle, and a frozen ten-scene evaluation using reference, stereo, and learned-depth observations. The experiments separate solver correctness under the scene assumptions from failure of those assumptions: fixed learned-depth bands often yield narrow but incorrect sets. The results identify what a specified scene class permits; they do not infer a continuum regularity or physical-scene guarantee from sampled predictions.
title: Sharp First-Hit Identification from Finite Depth Samples

Exact samples still give the sharp bound $Lh$ at $bL=1$, while above this threshold ambiguity need not vanish as sampling becomes arbitrarily dense. Any positive measurement uncertainty can destroy uniform stability at the critical threshold. We provide constructive examples, an exact rational validation oracle, and a frozen ten-scene evaluation using reference, stereo, and learned-depth observations. The experiments separate solver correctness under the scene assumptions from failure of those assumptions: fixed learned-depth bands often yield narrow but incorrect sets. title: Sharp First-Hit Identification from Finite Depth Samples

summary: Random forests (RFs) often achieve high prediction performance, but their ensemble structure can be difficult to interpret. Surrogate models and rule extraction methods offer interpretable approximations, yet guidance on selecting an appropriate method for a specific research question remains limited. We compared 12 methods for interpreting RFs, with a decision tree as a prediction-oriented reference, across 11 simulation settings and 67 benchmark datasets for regression and classification. Evaluation addressed prediction and structural similarity to the RF, model complexity, prediction performance, and runtime. Simulations additionally assessed explainability using known effect and noise variables. No method performed best across all objectives. For regression, SLIM provided the strongest general performance for prediction similarity or performance on test data, while a linear model offered a simpler global interpretation of linear effects when performance was comparable. For classification, inTrees achieved the strongest overall benchmark performance, with CTree and OC-CART providing useful alternatives. ART consistently produced the most compact representations. NH and SIRUS offered strong structural similarity for regression, while MRT most closely reproduced RF variable usage in the classification simulations, illustrating that prediction-oriented rankings do not necessarily identify the best structural explanation. Outcome-type restrictions, runtime limits, and method-specific failures reduced result availability for several approaches and should be considered alongside performance when selecting a method. Method selection should therefore be guided by the outcome type, anticipated data structure, and intended interpretability objective. Prediction similarity alone is insufficient for explaining an RF and should be considered jointly with structural similarity and model complexity.
title: Interpreting Random Forests: Comparing Surrogate Models and Rule Extraction Methods

summary: Evaluating Large Language Model (LLM) security agents requires reproducible environments whose workflow difficulty can be varied and whose failures can be diagnosed. We present VAST (Verifiable Adversarial Scenario Training & Evaluation), a declarative range compiler separating vulnerability scenarios from a compiler-introduced workflow-hardening layer. Following a post-hoc code and AST audit across all topics, the main benchmark retains 109 seed edges (45 with strict upstream CVE annotations), 72 family identifiers (62 under shared-HMAC relay grouping), 81 topic configurations (76 core plus 5 bounded execution models), and 1,387 instances (359 canonical four-gate-revalidated specs plus 1,028 seed variants) in a 42:39 partition. On the TopicServer compiler stratum, a budget-matched 270-episode prompt contrast across 10 compiled mechanism-family clusters (30 P2/P3/P4 instances, 40 turns, temperature 0.0) shows that glm-5.3, grok-4.7, and deepseek-v4-pro solve 12/90 instances under contract_only and 14/90 under generic_hint (cluster sign p=1.00), whereas supplying the shared workflow protocol in full_guide lifts completion to 76/90 (28/30, 23/30, 25/30; cluster sign p<=0.00391). On the separate ranges_v2 ledger, a 126-episode evaluation across 6 non-TopicServer workflows and multi-container Docker/Linux stacks solves 88/126 (69.8%) (28/42, 31/42, 29/42), while an 18-episode intervention on asynchronous Redis worker chaining (v2_02) lifts solves from 0/18 to 18/18 (100%) in 4-6 turns when installed worker modules are disclosed in GET /sched/directory. Finally, a three-seed (s in {42, 1024, 2025}) LoRA recipe comparison on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct across 37 lineage-disjoint families (231 episodes on 33 held-out instances) yields 0/33 for Base, 1.67 +/- 2.89 / 33 for Golden SFT, and 4.67 +/- 2.31 / 33 for Header-Recovery SFT, with all solves on v2_03.
title: VAST: Compiling Grounded Vulnerability Scenarios into Verifiable, Multi-Step Environments for Evaluating LLM Red-Team Agents

summary: [2.14.0] - 2026-11-15 Added A CI job compiles the library sources PydSEAMSlib and dseams-r build under Clang 22 with -Wsign-conversion -Wunneeded-internal-declaration -Werror , once without OpenMP or any optional backend and once with them, and builds those libraries with -Dwerror=true . The compiler-warnings workflow also runs on release/** branches. A Reproduce the paper catalog lists each seams-core figure and table with the command, the input frame, the printed numbers, and the Snakemake rule or asv class. Small rows run in the suite. Full rows run when -Dpaper_full=true . Each head-to-head names its committed CSV. A linux-64 pixi environment, cycles , holds Python 3.13 and bpy 5.3 for the Cycles molecule stills. pixi install -e cycles is enough: render_molecules.py finds that interpreter without MOLECULES_BPY . docs_render_molecules exits 77 only when no interpreter imports bpy . The environment adds lock entries and leaves the default environment's solve alone. A nucleation-pathway census reports primitive rings by size, both CHILL+ rules, Lechner-Dellago q6-bar, and diamond symmetry labels on every frame. The CHILL+ staggered and eclipsed edges are unchanged. Largest-cluster size and the Ic/Ih fraction are recorded for each definition. nucleation-pathway writes the table. input/nucleation/regenerate.py rebuilds the short mW quenches outside the work tree. A running molecular dynamics calculation can call the in-situ engine on each frame it chooses. The engine reports the primitive ring census. It also reports the published common neighbour ice labeling (CHILL) labels. The cage flags cover hexagonal and double-diamond cages. LAMMPS, GROMACS, OpenMM, i-PI, and the Atomic Simulation Environment attach through optional adapters. -Dplumed=enabled now errors. Live analysis does not use PLUMED. A top-level Comparisons page links the OVITO FindRings, freud, SQQ, and PLUMED head-to-head results already recorded in this book. Add seams_rings_chordless , which lists every chordless cycle of one size (3 to 12) in a neighbour graph as sorted canonical rows, the same for any thread count, with per-atom counts. It meets two induced half-paths in the middle, and the six-ring census in bench/ring_ice.c now calls it: 3.1 ms instead of 20.6 ms on 4096 mW molecules, one thread. Add a pinned head-to-head of cutoff neighbours, q4, q6, diamond, rings and local symmetry against mdapy, pyscal3, vesin, IRA and SQQ. Add optional IRA, SOFI and spglib symmetry reports for ice shells, hydrate cages and rings. Add pinned head-to-heads of 5^12 cages against ClavisCage TRACE and of q4, q6 and coordination against PLUMED. All twenty recordings embed their Odysee claims. The cages transcript adds the ice Ih hexagonal-cage census and the cubic double-diamond census, and keeps the clathrate lines. The brine transcript again includes the three-frame front beside the nacl census. The GROMACS overhead_s timer is machine-dependent. An unsigned-char CI job builds every target on x86_64 Linux with -funsigned-char and runs the suite on it, so code that reads a plain char as signed fails without an aarch64 runner. C API: seams_last_error_message , seams_system_natoms , seams_neighbours_nrows , seams_rings_nrings , and the length-checked seams_chill_plus_n , seams_q4q6_n , seams_rings_labels_n , and seams_rings_histogram_n . Every public declaration in seams.h now has a Doxygen block with parameters, ownership, thread safety, and an example. C API: seams_system_set_positions overwrites the coordinates, and optionally the cell, of a stored frame, and seams_system_box , seams_system_positions , seams_system_types , and seams_system_ids copy the stored frame back out through a const handle. seams_system_set_atoms reuses the storage of the frame it replaces, and keeps the id index when the ids are 1 to n, so loading 110592 atoms costs about the same as building the frame in C++. CI builds each engine plugin against the conda-forge engine and runs its engines-e2e tests,
title: d-SEAMS: Deferred Structural Elucidation Analysis for Molecular Simulations

summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Forty-eight entries are documented, thirteen of them confirmed defects in the source literature, among them: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7; a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients; a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset; a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten; a misprinted equation for trichromatic colour thresholds in Vorobyev & Osorio (1998); a row of Smith & Baker (1981) Table I whose pure water absorption exceeds its own diffuse attenuation; a sign misprinted in Duntley's (1963) equation for the apparent radiance along a slanted line of sight; a second factor of one half printed inside Fresnel's law in Gregg & Carder (1990). Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. Light through a Jerlov water type. The package: computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, or a slanted one in uniform water (Duntley 1963); converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors; gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m, and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers; integrates photosynthetically available radiation (PAR), or the photon flux over any other band or weighted by any spectral sensitivity, with depth; gives the spectrum at any depth and the effective Kd between two; and finds the depth at which PAR falls to 1 percent; ranks the Jerlov types by their distance from a measured Kd spectrum; carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models; converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient. Measurements it carries. summary: Existing feedback-based methods for online vision-and-language navigation (VLN) primarily learn from current episode outcomes, leaving previously acquired feedback underutilized. Inspired by human episodic memory, we propose R2A, an online VLN adaptation framework that continually reuses successful and failed navigation experiences for policy learning. Specifically, Success-Failure Memory (SFM) retains successful and failed navigation episodes with acquired feedback and retrieves task-relevant experiences based on incoming instructions, enabling historical feedback to guide subsequent navigation. Prior-Anchored Adaptation (PAA) learns from these experiences by reinforcing successful trajectories and suppressing failed ones relative to a frozen pretrained policy, while regularizing behavioral drift. Together, these modules enable continual feedback reuse and stable policy adaptation without source-domain data or expert supervision. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks, REVERIE, R2R, and R2R-CE, and five navigation backbones demonstrate consistent performance gains. On the REVERIE validation unseen split, R2A improves DUET's SR from 46.98% to 69.84% and SPL from 33.73% to 50.98%.
title: Remember, Replay, Adapt: Learning from Past Experience in Online Vision-and-Language Navigation

summary: Latent world models predict the future in an embedding space rather than in pixels. An encoder trained only to predict collapses and maps every observation to the same point, so existing models add a mechanism against collapse, such as a target network, a variance penalty or a distribution penalty. These mechanisms keep the embedding from collapsing, but they leave its distances without meaning, and the model cannot tell a reversible transition from an irreversible one. We propose Sense, a single cross-entropy loss over the directed distance $d(x\to y)=\sum_i \mathrm{ReLU}(y_i-x_i)$ that replaces these mechanisms. The loss avoids collapse on its own, and since the encoder no longer needs the predictor, the predictor is fitted afterwards to fixed embeddings by plain regression. On four pixel environments, the return distance learned by Sense detects irreversible transitions with an AUC between 0.95 and 1.00, where LeWorldModel stays between 0.39 and 0.59. On TwoRoom, the navigation benchmark of LeWorldModel, planning with Sense reaches the goal in 100% of episodes against 91% for LeWorldModel. As the goal moves farther away, the planning failure rate of every baseline grows, while that of Sense stays near zero in Cup, Cliff and Sokoban and is the lowest of all methods in Pendulum.
title: The Sense Paradigm for World Models

summary: An agent that stores facts over time eventually stores several versions of the same fact. Asked a value-agnostic question - "which team does X play for now?" - a similarity retriever cannot prefer the current version, because every version matches the entity the query names. StaleBench isolates this stale-retrieval failure on 892 real updating facts, with currency labels from the source (Wikidata validity years via TempLAMA), never from a retrieval score. Our central result is that retrieval metrics can rank memory policies backwards: a retention policy and its retain-everything control return the identical statement at rank 1 for every test query, yet differ by 29.5 and 65.6 points in reader accuracy on two readers when no date is shown. Contamination@5, the metric we add, ranks them correctly where current@1 and current@5 do not. Withdrawing the lexical anchor that statements carry costs deployed keying mechanisms tens of points of freshness; entity resolution on both the write path and the query recovers most of the loss. Three deployed systems (Mem0, Graphiti, LangMem) and a reimplemented ERASE each handle supersession differently, and no single scoring convention describes all four. We release the data, a frozen evaluator, and reference baselines.
title: StaleBench: Isolating Stale Retrieval in Agent Memory, and Pricing the Fix

We present a unified threat model, a taxonomy of attacks and defenses, and a review of evaluation benchmarks, and we align the area dimension by dimension with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) poisoning, prompt injection, and generative engine optimization (GEO). Coding 34 primary studies shows that only 26.5% of them involve the planning stage, and none performs an end-to-end poisoning evaluation on commercial products. To address this gap, we propose the agenda seeding attack, in which the attacker writes no instructions and only introduces a fictitious evaluation metric. Across 3,520 sandboxed research runs under the same budget, GEO and prompt injection are nearly ineffective, whereas agenda seeding makes the attacker's target the top pick in 16% to 28% of reports. Injection detection and query anchoring fail against it, verification prompting hurts utility, and our proposed provenance tagging preserves utility but can be bypassed by multi-site bait. Finally, we propose eight research directions.
title: Security of Deep Research Agents: Attack Surface, Defenses, Benchmarks, and Agenda Seeding against Research Planning

summary: Multi-objective Bayesian optimization (MOBO) traditionally aims to approximate the entire Pareto front, but, due to resource constraints, real-world deployment is often limited to testing a small, representative subset of solutions. Hence current methods first approximate the full front before selecting solutions, potentially wasting costly evaluations. We formalize this problem as Multi-objective Bayesian Optimization with Cardinality-aware Pareto Selection (MOBO-CAPS), where the goal is to identify a set of exactly M solutions with high hypervolume. We propose two practical cardinality-aware acquisition strategies: REHVI, a replacement-aware approximation to expected hypervolume improvement, and CHO-UCB, which constructs an optimistic M-point set by optimizing a collective UCB-based hypervolume objective. We prove a sublinear simple regret bound for the batched version of CHO-UCB, and empirically show that cardinality-aware acquisition design improves over standard MOBO followed by post-hoc subset selection across nine benchmarks.
title: MOBO-CAPS: Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization with Cardinality-Aware Pareto Selection

summary: The CAPSARII project advances a cyber-secure, ultra-low-power wearable platform and Internet of Battlefield Things (IoBT) framework to support real-time monitoring of military personnel and data-driven decision support. The architecture integrates smart-textile sensing, a body/squad area mesh, edge-deployed AI on secure RISC-V microcontrollers, and cloud/federated analytics for cross-mission learning and comparative studies. summary: Memory systems allow AI agents to persist information across interactions, making them more personalized and more capable on long-horizon tasks. This persistence introduces new risks: stored information can be disclosed in inappropriate contexts, resist correction or deletion, be retained beyond what users desire, or be poisoned to influence later agent behaviour. Yet memory systems are typically evaluated on task performance and efficiency alone. We argue that a memory system should instead be understood as the custodian of its user's persistent information, with responsibilities that extend beyond helping an agent complete its tasks, and that it should be evaluated holistically against all such responsibilities. We present Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems (HEAMS), an open-source framework for evaluating agent memory systems in this way. First, we state the responsibilities of agent memory systems as explicit behavioural desiderata spanning performance, efficiency, security, privacy, and user sovereignty. Second, we assemble a benchmark suite that covers these desiderata and acknowledge the gaps that remain. Third, we develop MilaMem, a prototype memory system, and a governance layer that can wrap any memory system, enabling controlled study of memory system design choices. Fourth, we compare memory systems across the full HEAMS benchmark suite. We find that no memory system leads every performance benchmark, and strong performance scores may coexist with poor privacy, user-sovereignty, and security scores. Governance strongly influences results: recall policies can reduce inappropriate disclosure at a cost in helpfulness, while both recall and retention policies improve poisoning resistance. Performance and efficiency benchmarks alone therefore cannot reveal how well a memory system meets its responsibilities. Code: https://github.com/milatechtransfer/heams
title: HEAMS: Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems

summary: Reasoning LLMs generate long outputs whose key--value (KV) caches occupy GPU memory for minutes. When memory fills, the server preempts requests, and a preempted request can repeatedly lose and recover its state while producing little new output. We call this behavior KV thrashing. In certain cases, existing systems leave more than a fifth of requests stalled for over a minute. Because preemption cannot be avoided without delaying admission, we ask how to make it productive. We present Stint, a serving system that preserves a preempted request's work, bounds how long it waits, and gives it fresh output after it returns. Stint stores fixed-length KV snapshots in a contiguity-first CPU pool with an exact-extent allocator, and moves them with fused K/V gather/scatter kernels and double buffering. Age-based readmission brings stalled requests back, and protection gives them a turn of fresh decoding before another preemption. Remaining-length estimates from decoding hidden states guide victim selection. On olympiad-math replays with Qwen3-32B on H200 GPUs, no request pauses for more than 50 seconds under Stint and p99 time per output token falls by 50.7\% relative to recomputation in the same engine. The replay as a whole finishes 10.7\% sooner (12.0\% higher throughput), because the requests that baselines starve no longer finish last.
title: Making Preemption Productive in Long-Output LLM Serving

summary: When an observed fact changes, an agent must identify and repair the decisions that depend on it while preserving unaffected outputs. Trace-derived graphs reduce reviewed decisions and estimated total cost, but omitted alternative supports and missing repair context can reduce complete-plan correctness. Paired ablations isolate the effects of edge deletion, spurious edges, transitive propagation and context scope. An exploratory enhancement supplies the existing record ID/field directory during extraction without revealing unread values or reference edges. We evaluate this enhancement on 60 fresh workflows with two repeats per model. On this fresh set, the directory-aware graph matches observed full-context complete-plan correctness for gpt-6.1-sol (100%) with an estimated 4.0% total-cost reduction, but reaches only 84.8% versus 99.6% for gpt-6-luna. summary: Video world models promise to predict the future of a scene from its present. Do current models keep this promise? We probe this question counterfactually. When a small change to the present flips the future, such as a box resting a few millimeters before or past a table edge, a model that tracks the state of the world must flip its prediction too. We build FlipTest, a three-level hierarchy of increasingly strict tests over 1,680 initial frames from 10 simulated and 15 real-world tasks. At the base, visual minimal pairs, two nearly identical frames whose true futures differ, test whether predictions change across the boundary; matched controls go further and test whether they change only where the future does; and dense sweeps, the strictest level, locate exactly where they change. All 11 video world models we evaluate fall short. The best averages 18.3% pair accuracy over real and simulated scenes, below the 25% of random guessing. Models flip as often on steps that leave the future unchanged as on steps that change it, and their response stays flat across the sweeps. On the same frames, a vision-language model is selective and traces a near S-shaped curve near the boundary, and a coding agent that measures the image comes close to the true boundary. This implies that the deciding information is in the frame, and video models just miss it. We therefore urge the community to rethink world modeling as pure video prediction. Next-frame prediction must do more than draw plausible pixels; it must also identify the causal states that control future dynamics.
title: The Flip Test: Video World Models Fail to Learn the World State

summary: World models learned from offline data allow an agent to plan without further interaction with the environment, but the sampling-based planners used with them handle safety constraints only by scoring or rejecting sampled action sequences. We instead pose safe planning in the latent space of a learned world model as a successive convex program (SCP), in which a learned discrete-time control barrier function is imposed as a constraint at every step of the horizon. SCP requires smooth dynamics, so we build the networks from smoothed MaxMin activations and spectrally normalised layers, and bound the resulting linearisation error in terms of the Lipschitz bound and the smoothing width. As SCP is a local method, we start it from a sampled plan. On two Safety-Gymnasium navigation tasks with offline data, this planner has fewer violations than MPPI and CEM drawing 128 times as many samples at equal wall-clock time in our main comparison, though not significantly, and earns greater return at longer horizons, and is much safer than SCP without a sampled start. SCP converged more often on Lipschitz-bounded models. Unlike sampling, it also reports at each step whether its plan is a feasible, first-order optimal KKT point of the planning problem in the model, or that no feasible plan was found nearby. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/youngers2006/scwm.
title: Successive Convexification in Learned World Models for Safe Offline Planning

summary: Timely urban-canopy information is essential for linking remote sensing with heat, mobility, and neighborhood planning. We developed an optical GeoAI workflow for Davis, California, using 2022 National Agriculture Imagery Program imagery (0.6 m RGB+NIR). DeepForest generated crown candidates; an NDVI threshold, non-maximum suppression, and box-prompted Segment Anything Model (ViT-B) produced a crown-anchored canopy surface. Analyses used the 25.92 km2 Census TIGER municipal boundary and a 100 m grid. The workflow retained 11,741 candidate crowns and mapped 7.71 km2 of canopy (29.8% of the city). On the identical extent, pixel precision was 0.804, pixel recall was 0.873, and 97.4% of candidate centers agreed with the 2022 USDA/CAL FIRE LiDAR-assisted canopy product (IoU 0.719; Dice 0.837; area recovery 108.5%). Approximately 49% of candidates occurred within 15 m of a road. Canopy was inversely associated with Landsat land-surface temperature (Spearman rho = -0.477; partial rho = -0.551 controlling for built probability), and spatial-lag modeling confirmed clear neighborhood structure. Two transparent attention surfaces combined canopy need with thermal and contextual indicators. The framework provides a reproducible, updateable screening layer that complements structural canopy products and municipal inventories while retaining assumptions, data provenance, and spatial diagnostics for planning interpretation.
title: Optical GeoAI and spatial modeling enable urban-canopy mapping and resilience screening in Davis, California

summary: Radio-frequency (RF) photonics enables broadband, phase-coherent sensing beyond the reach of purely electronic architectures, yet at a given optical carrier power its sensitivity is bounded by the standard quantum limit of the optical readout. Here, we experimentally demonstrate that this limit can be surpassed in both passive and active RF imaging modalities by encoding RF signals onto a bright phase-squeezed optical carrier and recovering them via balanced homodyne detection, while the RF front end, illumination, and image reconstruction remain classical. A unified measurement model shows that phase squeezing reduces the variance of the additive readout noise by a single factor $g$, yielding peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) gains of up to $2G$, where $G\equiv10\log_{10}(1/g)$: between $G$ and $2G$ for deterministic targets in active imaging when the classical noise of the echoes is negligible against the readout noise, and set by the ratio of scene noise to readout noise in passive imaging. We validate the model in an experiment in the 5--20 MHz band, in which synthesized RF scenes are replayed through a physical squeezed-light receiver. With 3 dB of squeezing, the PSNR improves by about 6 dB, close to $2G$, in the readout-noise-dominated regime of both modalities, and the model predicts the measured gains without free parameters. These results identify where squeezed-light readout benefits RF-photonic imaging: wherever the optical readout noise, rather than the scene or the RF front end, dominates the image error.
title: Quantum-Enhanced Passive and Active Radio-Frequency Photonic Imaging

A unified measurement model shows that phase squeezing reduces the variance of the additive readout noise by a single factor $g$, yielding peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) gains of up to $2G$, where $G\equiv10\log_{10}(1/g)$: between $G$ and $2G$ for deterministic targets in active imaging when the classical noise of the echoes is negligible against the readout noise, and set by the ratio of scene noise to readout noise in passive imaging. We validate the model in an experiment in the 5--20 MHz band, in which synthesized RF scenes are replayed through a physical squeezed-light receiver. With 3 dB of squeezing, the PSNR improves by about 6 dB, close to $2G$, in the readout-noise-dominated regime of both modalities, and the model predicts the measured gains without free parameters. These results identify where squeezed-light readout benefits RF-photonic imaging: wherever the optical readout noise, rather than the scene or the RF front end, dominates the image error.
title: Quantum-Enhanced Passive and Active Radio-Frequency Photonic Imaging

summary: Magnetically intercalated transition metal dichalcogenides are layered materials with highly tunable magnetic orders and unconventional transport properties. Here we report a surface-bulk magnetic dichotomy in $\mathrm{M}_{1/3}\mathrm{T}\mathrm{X}_{2}$, in which the surface and bulk favor distinct magnetic orders. In $\mathrm{Fe}_{1/3}\mathrm{Nb}\mathrm{S}_{2}$, angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) results are reproduced by an A-type antiferromagnetic electronic structure, while neutron scattering and bulk DFT+$U$ calculations identify stripe order as the bulk ground state. DFT+$U$ slab calculations resolve this contradiction by showing that relaxation of an Fe-terminated surface reverses the magnetic preference from stripe to A-type order. The same dichotomy recovers the $K$-centered Fermi-surface pockets that are observed in $\mathrm{Co}_{1/3}\mathrm{Nb}\mathrm{S}_{2}$ and $\mathrm{Co}_{1/3}\mathrm{Ta}\mathrm{S}_{2}$ but absent from previous bulk calculations. Notably, the surface-stabilized magnetic phase of $\mathrm{Fe}_{1/3}\mathrm{Nb}\mathrm{S}_{2}$ carries nonrelativistic spin splitting and can exhibit altermagnetic character. These results caution against the general association of ARPES signals with bulk magnetic states in these systems, and suggest surface-bulk magnetic dichotomy as a promising route to realize magnetic phases, including altermagnetism, that are not energetically favored in the bulk.
title: Surface-bulk magnetic dichotomy in intercalated transition metal dichalcogenides

summary: Whether electrical conductivity can be uniquely determined from magnetic measurements alone is a fundamental question in geomagnetic induction sounding. For a spherical conductor in the magnetoquasistatic model, we establish an equivalence between the complete Q-response and a restricted magnetic boundary operator, connecting geomagnetic induction to Calderon-type inverse boundary value theory. For axisymmetric conductivities, we derive exact representations of the zero-frequency zonal response derivatives as conductivity-weighted spatial moments. These formulas give an explicit interpretation of individual response derivatives, and completeness of the moment family yields conductivity uniqueness. For layered axisymmetric models with known shell interfaces and piecewise-constant radial dependence, we further establish uniqueness at a single nonzero frequency. Finite-dimensional subclasses also admit uniqueness and stability estimates from finitely many response coefficients at sufficiently low nonzero frequencies. These results identify complementary mechanisms for conductivity recovery from magnetic-only observations, while uniqueness for general three-dimensional scalar conductivities from ideal magnetic-only Q-response data remains unresolved.
title: Geomagnetic Q-Response Inversion as a Calderón-Type Inverse Boundary Value Problem

summary: Ensemble Kalman inversion (EKI) is a derivative-free and parallelizable method for parameter estimation in Bayesian inverse problems involving expensive forward models. It adapts Kalman filtering by repeatedly assimilating the observation data through an artificial dynamical system with identity state evolution and the parameter-to-observation map as its observation operator. However, its performance can be limited by ensemble collapse and confinement to the affine span of the initial ensemble. We propose an exploration-enhanced EKI framework that combines multiplicative covariance inflation with a projected-dropout correction of the ensemble mean. Inflation helps maintain ensemble spread, while projected dropout enables the mean to explore directions beyond the initial affine span. For linear inverse problems, we provide a discrete-time, finite-ensemble analysis of the resulting method and prove the least-squares objective converges exponentially to its minimum in expectation. Within the initial ensemble subspace, the contraction factor is independent of the conditioning of the inverse problem, and the limiting ensemble covariance provides a low-rank representation of the posterior covariance. Experiments on ill-conditioned linear systems, 100-dimensional nonlinear benchmarks, and a PDE-constrained barotropic flow inverse problem demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
title: Enhancing Exploration in Ensemble Kalman Inversion via Covariance Inflation and Projected Dropout

summary: Auroras provide remote optical observations of energetic electrons precipitating into the upper atmosphere, and whose energy distribution encodes key information about large scale magnetospheric processes. Recovering the underlying electron precipitation field from ground-based camera images of auroras remains a challenging inverse problem. Existing auroral tomography techniques are often limited to simplified static settings, discrete spatial and energy grids, or strong assumptions on the electron energy spectrum. We propose to model the dynamic auroral electron precipitation field via a temporally conditioned neural network. The state of the precipitation field at each frame is represented by a per-frame latent code driven by learned discrete dynamics. A shared decoder maps horizontal positions and latent states to electron energy spectra. The predicted flux is converted to multi-wavelength volume emission rates and rendered into camera images accounting for delayed emissions. We evaluate the method on synthetic dynamic auroral sequences and real multi-view auroral videos, showing that the proposed representation produces temporally coherent precipitation reconstructions and image projections consistent with the observations.
title: Spatiotemporal Reconstruction of Auroral Precipitations with Neural Fields

summary: We document the data reduction, reconstruction choices, and available uncertainty propagation underlying fifteen PHAROS stellar spectral energy distributions from 0.5 to 5000 nm. A catalogue timeline and a practical FITS guide introduce the available products, their column and extension conventions, and examples of reading, integration, and uncertainty display. Shared methods are presented once, including flux geometry, support-aware integration, X-ray likelihoods, the 2025 X/EUV luminosity relation, intrinsic Ly$α$ inference, airglow treatment, spectral junctions, and covariance-aware resampling. Target sections record the adopted observations and alternatives, including spatially separated binary components, unresolved system-level EUV measurements, direct EUVE constraints, optical stellar-twin transfer, and literature-anchored cases where new spectral inference is unsupported. The distinction between native measurement errors, conditional model intervals, empirical predictive scatter, and physical-method sensitivity is maintained. Signed measurements and nonnegative irradiation products are distinguished. Each target section concludes with the final nominal spectrum and its available uncertainty bounds on common axes. This library provides the detailed provenance and interpretation needed to accompany the catalogue paper and its machine-readable products.
title: The PHAROS Spectral Library: Data Processing, Spectral Reconstruction, and Uncertainty Propagation

summary: Methods for reliable in-situ estimation of small-strain damping ratio remain far less developed than those for in-situ shear wave velocity (Vs) measurements. For surface wave-based approaches, challenges with extracting damping ratios are caused by both difficulties associated with developing attenuation coefficients from recorded wavefields and complexities involved when interpreting their multimodal irregularities during inversion. This study presents a joint inversion framework for extracting shear damping ratio (Ds0) and Vs profiles from Rayleigh-wave attenuation and phase velocity data using a viscoelastic predominant-mode approach. Unlike conventional inversion, the proposed formulation identifies the mode contributing most strongly to the measured wavefield, allowing multimodal attenuation and dispersion data to be incorporated without explicit modal indexing. This approach has significant benefits for inverting attenuation data, whose modal behavior is much more irregular than phase velocity. A coupled inversion strategy is adopted to jointly estimate the Vs and Ds0 while addressing their different sensitivities to phase velocity and attenuation. The predominant-mode attenuation concept is first validated against two synthetic ground models of increasing complexity. The synthetic inversion results demonstrate the framework's ability to recover the Ds0 and Vs profiles and capture modal transitions associated with a low-velocity layer. The framework is then applied to active-source field data from Mirandola, Italy, where the fundamental mode dominates, and Bird's Landing, California, where a soft peat layer produces significant higher-modes. At both sites, the inverted Vs profiles agreed well with independent site characterization data, while the damping estimates exhibit physically plausible trends and provide site-specific information that complements empirical estimates.
title: Extracting Damping Ratio and Shear Wave Velocity through Joint Inversion of Rayleigh Wave Attenuation and Phase Velocity Data

summary: Learning the underlying probability distribution from samples is a core problem in statistics and applied mathematics. Generative models based on diffusion and flow matching learn a velocity field whose flow transports a known distribution to the data distribution. They produce novel, realistic samples, although the empirical learning problem is ill posed near the data distribution. Its minimizer transports the samples onto the training data, and small perturbations of the data change the velocity field strongly near the end of the flow. The observed generalization is often attributed to implicit regularization by the network parameterization, early stopping of the training, and the time integration during sampling. Explicit regularization has advanced the theory and computation of many inverse problems and has recently been proposed to prevent memorization in generative models. With a regularizer on the magnitude of the velocity, however, the field approaches the memorizing velocity unless the regularization parameter grows to infinity fast enough, and it then stays bounded by a constant that is small only for large parameters. We show that penalizing the derivatives of order $k$ of the velocity renders the $D$-dimensional empirical problem well posed uniformly in time if $2k > D$ and the training points are in general position. Our experiments in one and two dimensions discretize the velocity with splines and use direct solvers for the regularized least-squares problems to exclude optimization error. Refining the discretization in space and time changes the error of the Hessian-regularized flows only marginally, whereas without the regularizer the error tends to that of memorization. These flows generalize, with errors comparable to or lower than those of well-tuned kernel density estimates.
title: Explicit Regularization for Flow Matching
