summary: Hydroxide at neutral-to-alkaline pH and halides inhibit fungal laccases and limit their use in wastewater treatment. From GFN2-xTB cluster models of Trametes versicolor laccase (PDB 1GYC) we build a four-site Hubbard model of the His454-T3A-T3B-His452 junction of the trinuclear copper cluster and execute its charge-transfer dynamics on the Euro-Q-Exa quantum computer (IQM, 8 qubits, Trotterized circuits with Pauli twirling; 726 jobs). The charge-transfer frequency is measured to 3-5 meV, reproducibly over nine days and across changes of the device qubit map: hydroxide raises the charge-transfer energy of the crystal-geometry model by 92.0 +/- 2.2 meV (exact 87) and exceeds fluoride by 10.1 +/- 1.8 meV. A screen of charged probes in three dielectric models identifies Y116E; in the probe model the hardware resolves a reduction of the hydroxide penalty by 74 +/- 7 meV and of the halide penalty by 64 +/- 5 meV, acting on the site-energy gap rather than on the coupling. A real Glu116 (five conformers) with PROPKA protonation states and the coupled Asp456 gives a realistic reduction of 10-30 meV, with the same sign in 28 of 28 model combinations; the direction and ordering are the prediction, rate factors only an illustration. Scanning the on-site repulsion reverses the sign of the hydroxide effect, and a one-electron Hartree model reproduces the reversal: the measured dynamics is effectively single-particle. On a Fermi-Hubbard benchmark the hardware does not resolve electron correlation; it would need a contrast loss below 0.13 percent per CZ gate instead of the measured 0.34-0.54 percent.
title: Countering Anion Inhibition of Laccase Electron Transfer: Electrostatic Design, Charge-Transfer Dynamics on a Superconducting Quantum Processor, and Its Limits

summary: Different paths need not imply different preferences, trajectories also differ in how randomly actions are chosen. Many multi-reward inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) methods assume common action randomness and can confound it with preference heterogeneity. We introduce TRAIL-IRL, which clusters unlabeled trajectories using rewards for preferences and temperatures for action randomness. Its crossed mixture pairs each reward with a shared set of temperature levels, allowing action regularity to vary within preference groups. With centered and normalized rewards in a known finite-state environment, we establish the identifiability conditions under which the distribution of sufficiently long trajectories determines rewards, temperatures, mixing weights, and class counts up to relabeling. Under the same conditions and reward constraints, common-temperature reward mixtures with the same component count cannot reproduce a crossed mixture with multiple temperatures. We develop a generalized expectation-maximization algorithm and select class counts using the Bayesian information criterion (BIC). summary: Using a high-resolution GRMHD simulation of a magnetically arrested disk, we investigate the physical mechanism driving magnetic-flux eruption. The horizon-threading magnetic flux declines mainly in off-equatorial regions, whereas localized hot spots associated with magnetic reconnection appear near the equatorial plane around the onset of flux decline. A non-axisymmetric, magnetically supported low-density structure, which we identify as a magnetic bubble, expands radially and azimuthally within a pre-existing low-density channel in the filamentary accretion flow. Based on these findings, we propose a physical picture linking reconnection, bubble expansion, and horizon magnetic flux decline. The reconnection occurs in the pre-existing low-density channel, and may reconfigure the field and promote bubble expansion. Magnetic-pressure gradients provide broadly distributed outward support for the expansion, while magnetic tension contributes a localized outward force near the equator. Bubble expansion may limit gas replenishment, helping to maintain the low-density region and reduce the total pressure near the equator. This pressure reduction may facilitate equatorward electromagnetic energy transport. In the simulation, the polar electromagnetic energy flux reverses from poleward to equatorward near the onset of the horizon-flux decline. The equatorward transport is concentrated in the bubble sector and carries electromagnetic energy from the off-equatorial magnetosphere to the equatorial region. This energy supply may sustain localized reconnection and plasma heating as the eruption develops.

summary: A world model is trusted to answer "what if": how its world responds to an action it has never seen. We give a test of that trust for any action-conditioned world model: actions held out of training by design and scored against a known answer; whether forecast accuracy predicts accuracy on those actions; and the same structure given to simpler models. We run it in retail, where the action is a price and promotion plan, across 2,853 fitted models. First, forecast accuracy is a fair guide between kinds of model (rank correlation with error on new plans 0.32 to 0.66) and a poor guide between versions of one world model: where merchants plan into high-demand weeks the link reverses, down to -0.69. Second, training the world model to learn the effect of actions (JEPA pretraining, a latent consistency check, adaptation at the plan date) leaves its error on new plans unchanged. Third, in generated worlds the recorded regular price and three price rules improve it. Given the same rules, a log-linear model is best when its curve can match the truth; in a world whose curve lies outside the rules, the world model with the rules is ahead of the log-linear model with the rules in 36 of 40 worlds, and does as well without its recurrent cell. On real data (Breakfast at the Frat, The Complete Journey and M5) the rules lower the world model's error on pure price cuts deeper than any it saw (0.63 to 0.56 on the Frat; 0.45 to 0.44, within chance, on The Complete Journey), but not on lasting price moves. Fourth, a small share of random test plans helps every model a little. summary: Interactive video world models enable exploration through text and camera controls, yet direct object interaction requires finer control. Hands provide a natural interface, but translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses remains challenging because of complex hand-object dynamics and demanding real-time computation. To address these challenges, we introduce LynnReal-Hand, a hand-controlled video world model that unifies precise interaction modeling with efficient streaming generation. We curate 100K interaction clips spanning diverse real and synthetic environments and develop hand-aware supervision to improve fine-grained hand motions and object interactions. Building on this foundation, we learn a causal flow map for few-step generation and introduce region-aware score distillation that combines complementary video and image priors to refine interaction dynamics and visual appearance. To further reduce inference latency, we propose Ultra-Fast-VAE, a compact video decoder that preserves high reconstruction fidelity with substantially lower computational cost. Extensive evaluations on HandBench demonstrate superior hand-following accuracy and visual quality compared with existing approaches. Our full-sequence model achieves an FVD of 181.67 and a MANO Dice score of 93.02, while the three-step causal model maintains a MANO Dice score of 92.49. For real-time interaction, 540p streaming on a single H200 reaches 18.03 FPS with 741ms latency and an optimized peak GPU memory footprint of only 34.89GB. We will release the datasets, model weights, and the full training and inference code to support research on hand-controlled video world models.
title: LynnReal-Hand: Unlocking World Interaction with Hand Control

summary: When processor implementation details are unavailable, black-box microarchitectural reverse engineering helps security researchers identify hardware conditions related to security vulnerabilities. However, this process requires substantial manual effort to design experiments, develop test programs, and analyze results for each processor. We present ProcReverser, a multi-agent system that automates this process. ProcReverser uses execution feedback to improve experimental plans and test programs and identifies microarchitectural properties from measurements. We develop a comprehensive suite of property identification tasks focused on hardware mechanisms relevant to Spectre-class attacks, covering speculative execution, branch prediction, memory dependence, and cache behavior. We evaluate ProcReverser on the XuanTie C910, the gem5 RISC-V O3 CPU model, and the SiFive P550. ProcReverser achieves Pass@1 and Pass@5 scores of 81.3% and 93.8%, respectively, on C910, and 83.0% and 100.0% on gem5 O3. On the SiFive P550, ProcReverser further characterizes microarchitectural properties covered by the proposed task suite. These findings highlight the potential of automated microarchitectural reverse engineering to support processor vulnerability analysis and defense evaluation.
title: ProcReverser: Multi-Agent Black-Box Microarchitectural Reverse Engineering for Processor Vulnerability Analysis

summary: This dataset contains de-identified clinical, hematological, biochemical, questionnaire, and molecular data from a prospective longitudinal study investigating biological features associated with anxiety symptoms in medical students. The study included 33 medical students, classified into an anxiety-symptom group (n = 16) and a control group (n = 17) according to the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A). Clinical and biological measurements were collected at baseline and follow-up to explore changes associated with anxiety symptom severity over time. The dataset includes demographic characteristics, lifestyle-related variables, HAM-A total scores and symptom-domain assessments, hematological parameters (erythrocyte count, hemoglobin, and hematocrit), and serum cortisol concentrations. In addition, mitochondrial 7S RNA expression was evaluated by reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) in an exploratory subgroup of 10 participants (5 per group). The molecular dataset includes cycle threshold (Ct) values for mitochondrial 7S RNA and the reference gene RPLP0, as well as derived expression measurements calculated using the comparative 2⁻ΔΔCt method and log2 fold change transformation. The repository includes the complete clinical dataset, the RT-qPCR dataset, an Excel workbook containing the datasets, and a data dictionary describing the variables, units, and measurement methods. These data are intended to support transparency, reproducibility, and further research into the potential relationship between mitochondrial RNA regulation, neuroendocrine responses, and anxiety symptoms in the context of persistent academic stress. The findings and molecular measurements should be interpreted in light of the observational longitudinal design and the exploratory nature of the RT-qPCR subgroup analysis.
title: Mitochondrial 7S RNA Expression and Anxiety Symptoms Dataset

summary: TRANSREP — Experimental Results and Numerical Reproducibility (v1.3.0) This release provides experimental numerical data, analysis code, evaluation results, and reproducibility resources supporting the study Same Accuracy, Different Features: Checkpoint Alignment Changes Positional-Encoding Transfer Rankings in Vision Transformers . Version 1.3.0 extends the previously published v1.2.0 release with additional controlled experiments, depth- and token-resolved transfer analyses, and executable numerical verification tools. Experimental coverage Endpoint cohort E: 24 ImageNet-100 ViT-Base models across four positional-encoding configurations (Learned, Sinusoidal, 1D RoPE, and ALiBi), with six independent runs per configuration. Longitudinal cohort L: Twelve independently trained Learned and RoPE models, including upstream training trajectories, checkpoint-aligned transfer evaluations, and Oxford-IIIT Pets depth-resolved analyses. Completed-schedule cohort C: Twelve independently trained models under upstream-matched training schedules, with frozen-feature evaluations across five downstream classification tasks. Depth- and token-resolved analysis: 1,560 model-level probe scores across 13 representation depths and two token readouts (CLS and mean patch pooling). Epoch-300 evaluation: Frozen-feature readout comparisons and model-level upstream validation accuracies for twelve original endpoint models. External validation: Nine fixed public DeiT-III ImageNet-1k checkpoints comparing absolute positional embeddings with axial and mixed two-dimensional RoPE. Additional analyses: CKA representation comparisons, exploratory depth-dependent contrasts, and longitudinal late-readout comparisons. Numerical reproducibility The archive includes original numerical records, derived tables, analysis programs, and SHA-256 integrity manifests. A unified CPU-only verification procedure reproduces the supported score-level analyses, including the longitudinal and epoch-300 summaries, 65 depth-specific token-readout interaction contrasts, and 130 direct positional-encoding contrasts from archived B4-C model-level results. Verification instructions and software dependencies are provided in the root README and requirements-numerical.txt . The distribution does not include raw benchmark images, trained checkpoint weights, or large extracted feature arrays. Full model retraining and GPU feature extraction are therefore outside the scope of the portable numerical verification package. Code and licensing Original TRANSREP software is released under the MIT License. Original project-generated numerical data, figures, and associated documentation are provided under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International, subject to the provenance and third-party rights detailed in LICENSES.md . Source repository: https://github.com/djokobandjur/vit-pe-transfer Previous version (v1.2.0): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23986036 All-versions DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20368592
title: vit-pe-transfer: Positional Encoding and Checkpoint Alignment — Numerical Reproducibility (TRANSREP v1.3.0)

summary: This research archive presents a detailed continuum-model derivation of the electron anomalous magnetic moment g−2 within the electron sector of a broader common-continuum theoretical framework. It consolidates the historical Paper02 construction with the current Model113 formulation through A3.8328 and provides a complete derivational record of the intrinsic anomaly, second-normal residual dynamics, mechanical magnetic-current correction, gradient contribution, and the subsequently developed propagated electromagnetic-return channel. The current construction begins from the fixed electron structural parameter N2, the tangent-sector magnetic-current source, and the second-normal residual inventory Delta_infinity = 1 / [12 N2^2 (N2 - 1)]. The previously frozen mechanical magnetic correction is retained without modification. A distinct electromagnetic-return contribution is constructed through four separately typed factors: the electromagnetic-to-strong support ratio 1/N2, two-dimensional transverse spreading 1/(2 pi), the three-dimensional-to-two-dimensional ring-plane projection sqrt(2/3), and the inherited gradient enhancement 1 + 2/(pi N2). The resulting electromagnetic-return contribution is delta a_EM = Delta_infinity × (1/N2) × (1/2pi) × sqrt(2/3) × [1 + 2/(pi N2)]. Combining the inherited mechanical operator and the newly closed electromagnetic-return operator gives a_e = 0.0011596521805908756337882909101487… The archive explicitly preserves the earlier Paper02 precision-test failure rather than retrospectively rewriting the historical operator. The electromagnetic-return term was developed subsequently and is therefore reported as a new model-internal operator. Its close numerical agreement with the measured electron anomaly is treated as a retrospective consistency test rather than as a blind prediction. Particular attention is given to the provenance and physical identity of every factor, the separation of mechanical and electromagnetic readout channels, source-field-receiver typing, amplitude-versus-inventory distinctions, NoAlias constraints, NoDoubleCount constraints, and high-precision numerical reproducibility. The deposit contains the full derivation, historical operator record, Model113 provenance, numerical reproduction materials, formula freezes, and source-audit files intended to make the construction independently inspectable and reproducible.

summary: Choosing features is difficult with few labeled molecules, even for a tabular foundation model that learns in context. We study this problem with TabPFN for low-data molecular property prediction, separating input width, feature meaning, and predictive usefulness while keeping contexts, query molecules, and predictor settings matched. On ADME/Tox assays from Therapeutics Data Commons, endpoint-matched assay predictions improve a compact RDKit descriptor baseline, and a provenance audit shows that most audited query molecules already occur in the predictors' training sources. Across 77 FS-Mol development tasks and 157 held-out test assays drawn from ChEMBL, broad RDKit descriptor and fingerprint families provide a strong default, rank-averaging TabPFN with support-fitted fingerprint forests improves upon both models, and learned weighting of family predictions adds further gains at a larger prediction budget. A utility-trained selector builds a traceable 16-column input from 238 sourceassay predictors, improving upon the baseline while trailing wider representations and equalwidth structural SVD coordinates. Named outputs identify what each feature predicts and where it comes from. Their usefulness for a new assay is assessed alongside the other input features, and paired removal and replacement tests measure what each selected output contributes. Together, these studies offer a protocol for evaluating feature selection, representation choice, and data provenance with a fixed tabular foundation model for few-shot molecular property prediction.
title: Feature Selection for Tabular Foundation Models: Exploring Feature Utility in Low-Data Molecular Prediction

summary: Large-language-model agents now close the industrial predictive-maintenance loop, reading sensor windows, retrieving procedures and dispatching work orders. Two attack channels meet there: injected text in a retrieved document can hijack the decision, and a bounded sensor perturbation can corrupt the remaining-useful-life estimate behind it. Recent agent defenses police data provenance and tool privilege but cannot tell whether a prognostic quantity is physically plausible. ConfGuard is a reference monitor with a physics-grounded policy. Its conformal monitor tests each prediction, anchored to the asset's admitted history, against degradation physics: capped remaining life never rises and falls at most one cycle per cycle. Calibrating its threshold over whole asset trajectories lets the operator set the expected share of a clean asset's windows the running monitor escalates. A physics-policy validator checks the agent's maintenance-urgency decision against the decision a deterministic policy derives from the same interval. On all 10,196 C-MAPSS test windows the monitor cuts a covert attacker's reach on healthy assets from 0.529 to 0.046 and closes suppression of failing assets (0.151 to 0), escalating 0.027 of clean windows against a 0.05 target, while the fixed physical range it replaces leaves both attacks open. Behind a Qwen3-14B planner the composed monitors hold urgency-class injection to 0.00 and the universal sensor attack to 0.12, against 0.29 and 0.54 for a defended prompt. An adaptive attacker defeats a Mahalanobis detector on 0.504 of windows and adversarial training on 0.485. We report an attack class the projection misses.
title: ConfGuard: a physics-grounded reference monitor for predictive-maintenance large-language-model agents

Recent agent defenses police data provenance and tool privilege but cannot tell whether a prognostic quantity is physically plausible. ConfGuard is a reference monitor with a physics-grounded policy. Its conformal monitor tests each prediction, anchored to the asset's admitted history, against degradation physics: capped remaining life never rises and falls at most one cycle per cycle. Calibrating its threshold over whole asset trajectories lets the operator set the expected share of a clean asset's windows the running monitor escalates. A physics-policy validator checks the agent's maintenance-urgency decision against the decision a deterministic policy derives from the same interval. On all 10,196 C-MAPSS test windows the monitor cuts a covert attacker's reach on healthy assets from 0.529 to 0.046 and closes suppression of failing assets (0.151 to 0), escalating 0.027 of clean windows against a 0.05 target, while the fixed physical range it replaces leaves both attacks open. Behind a Qwen3-14B planner the composed monitors hold urgency-class injection to 0.00 and the universal sensor attack to 0.12, against 0.29 and 0.54 for a defended prompt. An adaptive attacker defeats a Mahalanobis detector on 0.504 of windows and adversarial training on 0.485. We report an attack class the projection misses.
title: ConfGuard: a physics-grounded reference monitor for predictive-maintenance large-language-model agents

summary: Lipophilic steroid and thyroid hormones circulate in human blood predominantly bound to high-affinity hepatic transport glycoproteins, leaving only a minute unbound fraction available for immediate cellular entry and receptor activation. According to the free hormone hypothesis, biological activity is governed primarily by this free hormone fraction rather than total circulating hormone concentrations. This structured IMRAD literature review, prepared at the Department of Biological Chemistry of Andijan State Medical Institute, examines the molecular biochemistry of the three principal specific transport proteins—thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG), sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), and corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG, or transcortin)—and analyzes how pathological states alter the ratio of free to bound hormone fractions. TBG and CBG belong to the serpin superfamily and utilize allosteric reactive center loop conformational transitions to regulate ligand release, whereas homodimeric SHBG binds testosterone, dihydrotestosterone, and estradiol with nanomolar affinity stabilized by divalent cations. Pathological conditions profoundly distort these carrier levels: hyperestrogenism and pregnancy elevate TBG and SHBG via sialylation and HNF-4α upregulation; insulin resistance, obesity, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and polycystic ovary syndrome suppress SHBG, elevating bioavailable free androgens; and hepatic failure, nephrotic syndrome, and critical illness reduce TBG and CBG, raising free cortisol and altering total hormone diagnostics. Evaluating free hormone indices alongside carrier protein biochemistry prevents diagnostic misinterpretation and clarifies tissue-level endocrine bioavailability.

summary: This dataset provides total column water vapor, vertical profiles, retrieval uncertainties, and averaging kernels derived from the mid-wave infrared (MWIR) channels of FengYun-4B/GIIRS using the Optimal Sequential Physical Retrieval System (OSPRS). FY-4B/GIIRS is the world’s first operational hyperspectral thermal infrared sounder in geostationary orbit, with the unique advantage of continuously scanning the atmosphere over East Asia on two hours basis during both daytime and nighttime. OSPRS is a full physical retrieval method based on the optimal estimation; it employs a sequential, multi-step retrieval strategy to reduce the non-linearity of the inverse problem at each step and to reduce the interference of non-target species on the primary retrieval targets (H2O, CO, and O3). The OSPRS algorithm is described in: Liang, Z., Gu, D., Li, X., Xu, Z., Cao, X., Bai, H., ... & Lau, A. K. (2025). An optimal sequential physical retrieval system for retrieving high-accuracy diurnal atmospheric gases from FY-4B/GIIRS: Theory, algorithm and evaluation. Remote Sensing of Environment, 328, 114901.  The full text is also available on the team’s webpage (http://dasagu.people.ust.hk/?page_id=108). The OSPRS water vapor products have been evaluated against ERA5 reanalysis, the TROPESS water vapor product retrieved from the polar-orbiting JPSS-1/CrIS instrument, and measurements from IGRA radiosondes and AERONET sun photometers. These evaluations demonstrate the utility of the products for characterizing spatial, temporal, and vertical variations in atmospheric water vapor and for monitoring extreme events, while identifying areas for further improvement. The detailed evaluation is provided in: Li, C., Liang, Z., Cao, X., Li, X., Xu, Z., Chan, W., ... & Gu, D. (2026). Comprehensive evaluation of atmospheric water vapor products retrieved from FY‐4B/GIIRS using the OSPRS algorithm. Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres, 131(12), e2025JD046022. https://doi.org/10.1029/2025JD046022. The full text is also available on the team’s webpage (http://dasagu.people.ust.hk/?page_id=108). The current dataset covers four representative months: April, July, and October 2023, and January 2024. Retrieval results covering longer time series will be released upon request or following further algorithmic improvements. Cloud screening was applied during preprocessing. It's also suggested implementing post-filtering based on "Number of iterations at convergence", "RMSE of the spectral fit residuals", and the "reduced cost function." It should be noted, however, that the definition of the "reduced cost function" in the current version is a subject of debate: some literature defines it as the cost function value at convergence divided by the number of spectral channels minus the number of variables in the state vector, whereas other sources suggest dividing it simply by the number of spectral channels. The current version of the product adopts the former approach, which may result in a higher calculated value for the reduced cost function. If you have any questions regarding the OSPRS algorithm or products, please contact Zhenxing Liang (zhxliang@ust.hk); if you have questions concerning the details of the water vapor evaluation in JGR-Atmospheres, please contact Cheng Li (clieo@connect.ust.hk).

OSPRS is a full physical retrieval method based on the optimal estimation; it employs a sequential, multi-step retrieval strategy to reduce the non-linearity of the inverse problem at each step and to reduce the interference of non-target species on the primary retrieval targets (H2O, CO, and O3). The OSPRS algorithm is described in: Liang, Z., Gu, D., Li, X., Xu, Z., Cao, X., Bai, H., ... & Lau, A. K. (2025). An optimal sequential physical retrieval system for retrieving high-accuracy diurnal atmospheric gases from FY-4B/GIIRS: Theory, algorithm and evaluation. Remote Sensing of Environment, 328, 114901.  The full text is also available on the team’s webpage (http://dasagu.people.ust.hk/?page_id=108). The OSPRS water vapor products have been evaluated against ERA5 reanalysis, the TROPESS water vapor product retrieved from the polar-orbiting JPSS-1/CrIS instrument, and measurements from IGRA radiosondes and AERONET sun photometers. These evaluations demonstrate the utility of the products for characterizing spatial, temporal, and vertical variations in atmospheric water vapor and for monitoring extreme events, while identifying areas for further improvement. The detailed evaluation is provided in: Li, C., Liang, Z., Cao, X., Li, X., Xu, Z., Chan, W., ... & Gu, D. (2026). Comprehensive evaluation of atmospheric water vapor products retrieved from FY‐4B/GIIRS using the OSPRS algorithm. Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres, 131(12), e2025JD046022. https://doi.org/10.1029/2025JD046022. The full text is also available on the team’s webpage (http://dasagu.people.ust.hk/?page_id=108). The current dataset covers four representative months: April, July, and October 2023, and January 2024. Retrieval results covering longer time series will be released upon request or following further algorithmic improvements. Cloud screening was applied during preprocessing. It's also suggested implementing post-filtering based on "Number of iterations at convergence", "RMSE of the spectral fit residuals", and the "reduced cost function." It should be noted, however, that the definition of the "reduced cost function" in the current version is a subject of debate: some literature defines it as the cost function value at convergence divided by the number of spectral channels minus the number of variables in the state vector, whereas other sources suggest dividing it simply by the number of spectral channels. The current version of the product adopts the former approach, which may result in a higher calculated value for the reduced cost function. If you have any questions regarding the OSPRS algorithm or products, please contact Zhenxing Liang (zhxliang@ust.hk); if you have questions concerning the details of the water vapor evaluation in JGR-Atmospheres, please contact Cheng Li (clieo@connect.ust.hk).

summary: In The Architectural Wall, I mapped how physical control systems hit an engineering ceiling across four epochs—from cast-iron lugs at the Tay Bridge (1879), to software bypass switches at Chernobyl (1986), to digital MUX bus latency at Deepwater Horizon (2010), culminating in probabilistic cross-syntax AI models "smoothing over" analog anomalies until kinetic failure occurs (Epoch IV)—and resolved it with The Minos Gate™ (a hardware-level 0V physical cutoff outside the compute loop). This sequel demonstrates what happens when that exact same failure mode scales from industrial hardware to sovereign statecraft and critical national infrastructure.

summary: A corpus of 219,384 Indian recipes across 378 source sites, with parsed ingredients in English/Roman, a 17-class allergen surface carrying an explicit unassessed sentinel, and estimated dish-level micronutrition; a typed knowledge graph of 222,537 nodes and 6,449,114 edges across 17 node types and 22 relation types; a 67-query retrieval benchmark with knowledge-graph-derived gold sets; a synthetic collaborative interaction log; and, since 0.11.0, an occasion-registry and dietary-rule context layer imported as silver data with structured citations (never executed as constraints), plus a recipe-ID crosswalk to a historical snapshot. The food-composition layer uses the IFCT 42-nutrient schema but contains no IFCT and no Indian composition data; its values are USDA SR Legacy and UK CoFID. Two-tier release. Structured, factual and derived fields are published under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 with per-recipe source attribution. Raw recipe prose is not redistributed; a rehydration index of source URLs and SHA-256 text digests is published instead, together with a re-fetch script. Known defects are published, not hidden. An independent allergen and diet audit ships with the data. See the datasheet before use, and do not use the allergen flags for end-user safety decisions.

summary: Code, benchmark and per-run results for the article Drive around or cut holes? Obstacle-aware coverage paths and controlled-traffic tramlines for paddocks with scattered trees and rock outcrops . The release extends the open-source coverage planner Fields2Cover (v2.1.1) with gate-anchored routing, an obstacle model for trees and rock outcrops, a curvature-bounded drive-around strategy, a straddle strategy for low obstacles, a raster section-control model and a controlled-traffic (CTF) tramline model. It contains the benchmark generator and runners, the per-run results of experiments E1 (855 layout-width cases), E2 (180 native Fields2Cover configurations), E3 (straddling low outcrops) and E4 (CTF tramline layouts), and the analysis scripts that regenerate every number, table and figure of the article. The simulation experiments were run on the Nectar Research Cloud, supported by the NCRIS-funded Australian Research Data Commons (ARDC).
title: obstacle-aware-coverage: Fields2Cover extensions, benchmark and data for obstacle-aware coverage paths and controlled-traffic tramlines

summary: Code, configurations, run manifests and results of the study "String Stability of Learned Car-Following Models: Audit, Differentiable Penalties, a Certified Hybrid and Corridor-Level Validation" (Mathematics 2026, 14(22), 4152, https://doi.org/10.3390/math14224152): an audit of the equilibrium (string) stability of learned car-following models, differentiable stability penalties, a residual hybrid with an a priori certificate, and the validation of the laws on SUMO corridors of NGSIM I-80 and US-101. The archive holds the code, the published tables, figures and report, and the run outputs they are computed from (training-run metrics and audits, per-event closed-loop metrics, corridor-run metrics and the compact speed fields of the figures, scenarios, law files, calibrations and fold definitions). The raw data, the extracted events and the simulated trajectories are not included; the README (section Reproduce) gives the three levels of reproduction and the data access steps.

summary: Replication package for an exploratory observational panel analysis of pesticide use and real gross crop production value during 2000–2022. The core panel contains 3,882 observations from 177 countries and territories; common labor/capital comparisons retain 3,610 observations from 163 reporting units. Contents include selected provider source extracts, analysis-ready panels, provenance, variable definitions, sample keys, Python processing and estimation scripts, expected numerical results, and table/figure source data. Version 1.0.1 updates creator and citation metadata only; analytical files are unchanged from version 1.0, which was replayed offline with 38 numerical tables/panels matching the original results within recorded tolerances. The outcome is gross crop production value, not profit or value added; models do not identify causal pesticide returns. Source statistics were retrieved from FAOSTAT and World Bank CCKP/ERA5 on 11 November 2026. Both authors contributed equally. No external funding or competing interests were declared. Original code and documentation are MIT-licensed; source data retain their providers’ terms. See README.md, LICENSE_CODE.txt and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md in the archive. This record contains data and code, not the unpublished manuscript.

summary: Radar image restoration is often challenged by system blur and speckle noise, which degrade target visibility and structural fidelity. In this work, we evaluate three restoration approaches—Richardson–Lucy deconvolution with total variation regularization (RL+TV), Deep Image Prior (DIP), and a new attentionenhanced framework combining DIP with the Convolutional Block Attention Module (DIP+CBAM). A point-spread function (PSF) was extracted from a measured corner reflector and used to simulate realistic degraded radar images. Experimental results show that RL+TV provides limited recovery of fine details, achieving a PSNR of 14.66 dB and SSIM of 0.4969. DIP substantially improves reconstruction quality (PSNR 19.39 dB, SSIM 0.5267), benefiting from the implicit prior of untrained networks. The proposed DIP+CBAM method further enhances performance, reaching the highest PSNR (19.54 dB) and SSIM (0.5361). These findings demonstrate that integrating attention mechanisms into DIP offers a more effective prior for radar image restoration and leads to clearer, more structurally accurate reconstructions

summary: We reassess selected neutral oxygen–gallium-vacancy configurations in GaN using archived CP2K/PBE calculations and new endpoint evaluations. Five components comprise a 72-atom host, substitutional oxygen, a gallium vacancy and separately selected two- and three-oxygen vacancy complexes, C2 and C3. Although the original static energies are reconstructable, fixed-coordinate energy-and-force evaluations using one recorded executable reveal failures of the retained force criteria for the vacancy, C2 and C3. Small total-energy changes therefore do not establish acceptable endpoints. Bounded C2/C3 optimizations followed by separate complete energy-and-force evaluations now support selected-protocol endpoints. Explicit combined review of original geometry criteria and current force/electronic evidence also admits the host and substitutional-oxygen endpoints. Direct subtraction of these four raw energies gives b3 = 1.76504 eV for the selected host-balanced C2/C3 comparison. The vacancy repair fails its first updated-geometry SCF after 300 iterations, producing no qualified new endpoint; cumulative A2/A3 results remain unaccepted. The evidence preserves a C2 interruption after its complete converged step, a C3 wavefunction overwrite resolved through its documented backup, and a corrected provenance error in an excluded one-oxygen complex. This is a traceable numerical case and a restricted association descriptor, not a new discovery of oxygen–vacancy binding. Global structural/electronic minima, calibrated numerical uncertainty, capture kinetics and an oxygen-removal process are not established.\n\nThis technical report is accompanied by supplementary evidence and a metadata-redacted analysis dataset with scripts to reconstruct core tables and figures from saved CP2K outputs. It is not a complete DFT rerun environment. External peer review has not been completed. The selected result is a limited numerical case, not a novelty claim about oxygen–vacancy binding.
title: Selected neutral oxygen gallium-vacancy association in GaN: a technical report with reconstructable data
